title: Free time is not free.
dek: A student week has 51 free hours in it, more than school takes. Money can wait in an account. An hour gets spent the moment it arrives.
whyThisIdea: Am sărit peste ideile 7–9 din backlog pentru că se suprapun cu articolele despre Monday, identitate și telefon, și am luat #10 („Free time is the thing you are actually investing”): azi e sâmbătă, ziua cu cel mai mult timp liber, și închide firul articolelor despre bani (Psychology of Money, economisitul la 18 ani) cu partea pe care n-o scrie nimeni pe hârtie - orele. Singura cifră externă e verificabilă (2,6 ore/zi la TV, American Time Use Survey 2024, BLS), restul e aritmetică proprie, verificată.

entry.title: Free time is not free.
entry.dek: A student week has 51 free hours in it, more than school takes. Money can wait in an account. An hour gets spent the moment it arrives.
body: “You can save money for later. An hour you can only spend.”

Have you ever asked yourself what you actually own the most of? Not money - at my age that question has a very short answer. I mean time. Today is a Saturday, the day of the week with the most of it, and I already caught myself spending the first hour of it on nothing I could name. So the question is: if free time is the one thing I have plenty of, why do I treat it as if it cost nothing? Let’s start from the beginning.

On this blog I have already written about money twice, about compound interest in the review of The Psychology of Money and about saving $100 a month at eighteen. Both times the hidden ingredient was the same - time. Buffett’s number only works because he started at 10, the $100 only works because it has 47 years in front of it. And it made me think that I was always looking at the money side of the sum, when the thing doing the real work is the side I never write down. Nobody I know keeps a list of their hours the way a company keeps a balance sheet.

Firstly, let’s split the phrase in two, the way I like to do. “Free” and “time”. The time part is honest. The “free” part is where the trick is. It says the hour costs nothing, because nobody sends you a bill for it. But every hour has a price, it is just not paid in money, it is paid in all the other things the same hour could have been. And there is one big difference from money that I think we forget: <u>money can wait in an account, an hour cannot wait anywhere</u>. You cannot put this Saturday aside and use it in March. Every hour gets spent the moment it arrives, the only decision is on what.

Secondly, let’s count how much of it there is, because I never had. I built my own week as a student, and these are my guesses, not a study. A week has 168 hours. Sleep 8 a night and 56 are gone. School and homework, about 8 hours on each of the 5 weekdays, take 40. Eating, washing, getting from one place to another, say 3 hours every day, another 21.
168 - 56 - 40 - 21 = 51 free hours a week
Read that again: in my own example there are more free hours in a week than school hours. Saturday alone, with no school, has 24 - 8 - 3 = 13 of them. I complain that I do not have time for things, and the count says I have 51 hours a week that nobody has claimed (I mean sure, nobody except me).

Now let’s put it a little bit in perspective with a real number. The American Time Use Survey, which the US Bureau of Labor Statistics runs every year, found that in 2024 people aged 15 and over spent on average 2.6 hours a day watching TV - more than any other leisure activity. I am not American and it is an average across all ages, so it is not my number, but let’s run it anyway.
2.6 hours × 365 days = 949 hours a year
949 hours ÷ 16 waking hours a day = about 59 waking days
So almost two months a year, awake, in front of one screen. From 18 to 30 that is 12 × 949 = 11.388 hours (yes, you read that right).

And here is where it connects back to money. Hours do something similar to compound interest, they are only slower to see. An hour a day spent on one skill does not feel like anything on day one, exactly like the first $100 in the account. But take half of that TV time, 1.3 hours a day, and give it to one thing - a language, an instrument, code.
1.3 hours × 365 days = about 475 hours a year
1.3 hours × 365 days × 5 years = more than 2.370 hours
I am not going to promise you what 2.370 hours of anything turns you into, because I do not know, and I do not trust anybody who says they know. But I do know it is not nothing. The hours are the deposit, and the skill is the interest.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Not every free hour is waiting to be invested. Some of it is rest, and rest is not a waste - a tired person does everything badly, studying included. Some of it is friends and family, and the Psychology of Money review closed on a quote that puts exactly those things above any number. The problem is not the hours spent on nothing important. The problem is the hours spent on nothing I chose. Watching a film with a friend on purpose and scrolling for an hour because the phone was close are the same 60 minutes on paper and two completely different things.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. Today, this Saturday, I will write down what each of my 13 free hours actually went on. Not to judge them, just to see them, because I have never once looked at my hours the way I look at the money in my account. Next Saturday I will do it again and compare the two lists. If anything changes, I expect it to be in the hours I picked, not in the hours that just happened to me.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I believe the idea is right, but I do not fully like the language I used to say it. Calling free time an “investment” turns every evening into a spreadsheet, and I can already imagine a version of me who feels guilty for watching a match because the hour “did not return anything”. That version is not happier, he is just tired in a more organised way. And I have to admit that I picked the 2.6 hours of TV because it is an easy target - my own number is probably the phone, and I have not measured it yet. So the honest version is smaller: not every hour has to earn something, but every hour should at least be mine.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“You can save money for later. An hour you can only spend.”
